paragraphs: The paper studies how to build neural networks whose outputs cannot change more than their inputs, as measured by a Lipschitz constant of one. Controlling this sensitivity matters for adversarial robustness: small changes to an input should have a bounded effect on the network. The contribution concerns architectures designed to satisfy that mathematical constraint.

The authors view residual networks through continuous-time dynamical systems. This perspective provides a general construction for 1-Lipschitz networks and places some earlier approaches inside the same framework. They then show that residual-network flows derived from convex potentials produce 1-Lipschitz transformations. This result motivates a building block called the Convex Potential Layer.

Experiments across several datasets demonstrate that the resulting architecture can scale and provide benefits for provable defenses against adversarial perturbations measured with the Euclidean norm. The theoretical construction and empirical evaluation serve different purposes: the construction establishes controlled sensitivity, while the experiments investigate its usefulness in practical networks. The result connects architectural design to a mathematically grounded form of robustness.
icml-2022-a-dynamical-system-perspective.tldr: A dynamical-systems view of residual networks yields 1-Lipschitz architectures and convex-potential layers for provable adversarial defense.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows represent complicated probability distributions by composing transformations that can be reversed. Their linear layers must balance expressive power with the ability to compute inverses and track changes in probability density. This paper introduces a family of invertible linear layers based on butterfly matrices to address that balance.

Butterfly layers can theoretically represent complex linear structures, including permutations and periodic patterns, while allowing efficient inversion. The authors use this combination to construct ButterflyFlow. The motivation is that a layer capable of expressing these structures can better match patterns found in data without making the flow prohibitively expensive to run.

The experiments report strong density estimation on natural-image datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet at 32-by-32 resolution. On structured datasets involving galaxy images and MIMIC-III patient cohorts, ButterflyFlow achieves significantly better log-likelihoods than the relevant baselines. It also uses less memory and computation in the reported comparisons. These findings support butterfly layers as a practical way to combine structured expressiveness with computational efficiency.
icml-2022-butterflyflow-building-inverti.tldr: ButterflyFlow uses efficiently invertible butterfly layers to improve density modeling and reduce computational costs in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Estimating counterfactual outcomes means predicting what would happen under a different treatment history. For observations collected over time, this requires accounting for changing variables that influence both treatment assignment and outcomes. The paper develops a transformer architecture to capture complex dependencies across long histories, which can be challenging for the LSTM-based methods it discusses.

The Causal Transformer combines three subnetworks, separately processing time-varying covariates, previous treatments, and previous outcomes. Cross-attention connects these streams so that the model can represent interactions among them. Its custom training procedure includes a counterfactual domain confusion loss, intended to make learned representations useful for predicting the next outcome while making the current treatment difficult to predict.

That training objective aims to reduce confounding bias by balancing representations across treatment assignments. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets show better performance than the compared baselines. The stated contribution therefore combines a model for long-range temporal relationships with a training mechanism directed at confounding, supported by empirical improvements in counterfactual outcome estimation.
icml-2022-causal-transformer-for-estimat.tldr: The Causal Transformer combines interacting temporal subnetworks with a balancing loss to improve counterfactual outcome estimation.

paragraphs: Aligning time series requires adjusting when events occur while preserving their temporal ordering. The paper focuses on smooth, invertible warping functions that provide this kind of transformation. Such warps can be generated by integrating a velocity field, but training a model containing them also requires derivatives of the resulting transformation with respect to its parameters.

Those derivatives are difficult to handle because the transformation is defined through the solution of a differential equation. The authors derive closed-form expressions for both the solution and its gradient when the velocity field is continuous and piecewise affine. This gives a direct mathematical treatment for that specified class of velocity functions.

The paper also provides optimized CPU and GPU implementations. Experiments on several datasets evaluate joint time-series alignment and the model's ability to generalize to unseen data, reporting significant improvements in efficiency and accuracy. The contribution links the mathematical form of the warp to its trainability: choosing a suitable velocity-field family makes both transformation and parameter sensitivity available in closed form.
icml-2022-closed-form-diffeomorphic-tran.tldr: Closed-form time-warp solutions and gradients for continuous piecewise-affine velocity fields improve time-series alignment efficiency and accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper introduces CRAFT, a sampling method that combines sequential Monte Carlo with variational inference based on normalizing flows. The sequential sampler works across annealing temperatures, while the learned transformations move samples between those stages. This brings a trainable transport mechanism into a sampling procedure rather than treating sampling and flow learning as separate tasks.

Each flow is trained using a KL-divergence objective for its particular transition between temperatures. The objective is itself estimated using the combined flow and sequential Monte Carlo approximation. Thus, the current sampling approximation supplies information for learning transformations that transport samples through the annealing sequence.

The authors provide conceptual arguments and multiple empirical examples showing improvements over Annealed Flow Transport Monte Carlo and MCMC-based Stochastic Normalizing Flows. They also incorporate CRAFT into particle MCMC and obtain highly accurate results on a challenging lattice field theory example. This last result demonstrates how a learned sampler can contribute within a broader Monte Carlo method, extending the practical role of the learned transport maps.
icml-2022-continual-repeated-annealed-fl.tldr: CRAFT trains normalizing flows within sequential Monte Carlo to improve transport between annealing stages and sampling performance.

paragraphs: Training a model can expose information about its training data, so private optimization must balance predictive usefulness with privacy protection. This paper proposes differentially private proximal coordinate descent, or DP-CD, for composite empirical risk minimization. Its central idea is to exploit differences between gradient coordinates when designing private optimization steps.

The authors develop an analysis of inexact coordinate descent that yields utility guarantees. Their results show that larger step sizes allow DP-CD to benefit from imbalance across gradient coordinates and potentially outperform private stochastic gradient descent. They also establish lower bounds under coordinate-wise regularity assumptions, which DP-CD nearly matches. These bounds help characterize how much improvement is possible within that setting.

For implementation, the theory supplies separate gradient-clipping thresholds for individual coordinates, avoiding costly tuning of those thresholds. Experiments using real and synthetic data support the theoretical findings and compare favorably with DP-SGD. The contribution ties together an optimization method, an account of when coordinate imbalance helps, and a practical rule for configuring gradient clipping.
icml-2022-differentially-private-coordin.tldr: Private coordinate descent can exploit gradient imbalance to improve utility, with near-matching lower bounds and theory-guided clipping thresholds.

paragraphs: Distribution regression learns predictions whose inputs are probability distributions. A central challenge is representing each distribution in a way that preserves the properties relevant to prediction. Existing kernel mean embeddings offer strong statistical foundations, but the metric they implicitly use, maximum mean discrepancy, may be less suitable for capturing geometric relationships between distributions.

The paper proposes a representation based on Sliced Wasserstein distance, drawing on optimal transport. It uses this representation to build a kernel ridge regression estimator. The aim is to incorporate a geometry-sensitive comparison of distributions while retaining the kind of statistical guarantees available for established kernel approaches.

The authors prove universal consistency and excess risk bounds for the proposed estimator. These results address its statistical behavior, including the challenge that distributions are themselves observed through samples. Preliminary experiments demonstrate effectiveness and compare the method with MMD-based estimators. The contribution is therefore primarily a theoretically supported alternative representation, with initial empirical evidence for using transport geometry in distribution-level prediction.
icml-2022-distribution-regression-with-s.tldr: Sliced Wasserstein kernels bring optimal-transport geometry to distribution regression while supporting consistency and excess risk guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper investigates quantum circuits that learn representations of graphs. It introduces equivariant quantum graph circuits, or EQGCs, whose design incorporates the relational structure of graph data. The framework organizes several circuit subclasses and includes existing proposals within a common mathematical description.

The authors prove that the studied subclasses can universally approximate functions over a bounded graph domain. This establishes a broad representational capability within that domain. It also supplies a theoretical basis for investigating quantum graph-learning models, including the possibility of capabilities beyond classical approaches. That possible advantage remains a direction suggested by the framework.

A dedicated synthetic-data experiment supports the expressive-power results. The authors also observe that performance scales well with circuit depth and that the tested models do not encounter barren plateau issues. These observations concern the evaluated setting, while the approximation theorem concerns representational power. Together, they provide complementary reasons to investigate EQGCs: a unified architecture family, a formal expressiveness result, and encouraging empirical behavior.
icml-2022-equivariant-quantum-graph-circ.tldr: Equivariant quantum graph circuits unify graph-learning architectures and offer universal approximation results on bounded graph domains.

paragraphs: When external rewards are rare, an agent can explore by rewarding itself for prediction errors. However, unpredictable events can keep producing errors even when there is nothing useful left to learn. An agent may repeatedly trigger such randomness and become stuck in what the paper calls a noisy-TV trap.

The proposed aleatoric mapping agents predict both the mean of a future state and its aleatoric uncertainty, meaning the unpredictability associated with the transition. These separate predictions aim to reduce curiosity rewards for transitions that remain unpredictable, including randomness caused by the agent's own actions. The mechanism therefore adjusts the reward according to the kind of uncertainty behind a prediction error.

Across a range of environments, these agents avoid action-dependent stochastic traps that immobilize conventional curiosity-driven agents. The experiments also show that other common exploration approaches, previously considered immune to agent-induced randomness, can become trapped. The findings make uncertainty estimation relevant both to constructing curiosity rewards and to evaluating claims that an exploration strategy resists stochastic distractions.
icml-2022-how-to-stay-curious-while-avoi.tldr: Aleatoric mapping agents estimate unpredictable transitions so that curiosity rewards are less likely to trap them in action-induced randomness.

paragraphs: Public prediction APIs face a tension between helping legitimate users and supplying information that could help an attacker copy the model. Withholding uncertainty estimates or explanations can reduce usefulness and transparency. This paper studies defenses that make copying harder while preserving useful model outputs and keeping computational costs manageable.

The proposed approach, gradient redirection, aims to steer the training updates of an adversary in a chosen direction. Its core is an efficient algorithm with a proof of optimality for that steering task. The full defense, called GRAD^2, combines this algorithm with improved surrogate networks and a coordinated defense strategy.

The authors report that GRAD^2 outperforms the best prior defenses while introducing small utility trade-offs and low computational overhead. They also demonstrate that gradient redirection can induce arbitrary behavior in the adversary's model. That demonstration expands the proposed role of a defense from merely degrading a stolen model to influencing what it learns. The practical claim rests on the reported defense comparisons and behavioral demonstrations.
icml-2022-how-to-steer-your-adversary-ta.tldr: GRAD^2 redirects a model thief's training updates, improving reported defenses with small utility trade-offs and low computational overhead.

paragraphs: Neural retrieval systems score how relevant a document is to a query. Cross-attention models represent the query and document jointly, while dual encoders represent them separately. Cross-attention often performs better empirically. This paper asks whether that gap reflects an inherent restriction in dual encoders or problems with how they are trained.

The theoretical result shows that dual encoders can represent a broad class of score distributions when their embedding dimension is sufficiently large. This establishes a capacity result under an explicit dimensionality condition. It gives a reason to investigate training behavior rather than attributing every observed accuracy gap to the separate-embedding design.

The empirical analysis finds that dual encoders may overfit to spurious correlations in training data and consequently perform worse on test examples. The authors propose a distillation strategy to mitigate that behavior and demonstrate its effectiveness on MSMARCO-Passage and Natural Questions. The findings connect a theoretical account of model capacity with a practical explanation for underperformance and a training-based remedy.
icml-2022-in-defense-of-dual-encoders-fo.tldr: Dual encoders have broad capacity with sufficiently large embeddings, and targeted distillation can mitigate harmful training correlations.

paragraphs: Graph-learning models are often used to discover meaningful structure, making their explanations part of their scientific value. Methods that explain an already trained model can produce unstable interpretations or highlight features that only happen to correlate with the task. The paper develops Graph Stochastic Attention, or GSAT, to incorporate interpretation into learning itself.

GSAT follows the information bottleneck principle. It adds randomness to attention weights to suppress information from graph components irrelevant to the task, while learning attention with less randomness for relevant components. The resulting selected subgraphs provide the interpretation. Under stated assumptions, the authors prove that these subgraphs exclude patterns that are spuriously correlated with the task.

Experiments across eight datasets report improvements over state-of-the-art methods of up to 20% in interpretation AUC and 5% in prediction accuracy. These are maximum reported improvements rather than uniform gains across every dataset. The results support the possibility of improving interpretability and prediction together through a learning mechanism that controls which graph information passes through.
icml-2022-interpretable-and-generalizabl.tldr: GSAT uses stochastic attention to select explanatory subgraphs, with conditional guarantees against spurious patterns and empirical gains in interpretation and accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how deep networks might learn through mechanisms compatible with strong feedback between neural layers. Existing biologically motivated credit-assignment methods often require extremely weak feedback signals. The authors argue that this requirement is problematic in noisy settings and conflicts with evidence that top-down feedback can substantially change neural activity.

Building on deep feedback control, they let a controller drive network activity toward the supervised target. Learning then changes the weights to reduce how much feedback the controller must supply. This reframes optimization as minimizing the control needed to produce the desired output. The authors also show that strong feedback permits simultaneous learning of forward and feedback connections using rules local in both space and time.

Experiments on standard computer-vision benchmarks show performance competitive with backpropagation and robustness to noise. Alongside the theoretical analysis, these results support control minimization as an alternative account of credit assignment. The contribution concerns a learning mechanism that accommodates substantial feedback while retaining gradient-based learning and local updates.
icml-2022-minimizing-control-for-credit-.tldr: Strong-feedback learning can train networks by reducing the control needed to reach target outputs, using local learning rules.

paragraphs: Conventional neural networks usually map inputs to outputs through a fixed order of computation. That makes it difficult to express a structured problem in which variables can influence one another in different directions. This paper introduces undirected neural networks, combining the modular representation of factor graphs with the function-learning capabilities of neural networks.

The framework specifies computations that can be performed in different orders. With particular choices, it includes and extends feed-forward networks, recurrent networks, self-attention, auto-encoders, and architectures with implicit layers. This common formulation allows the authors to investigate how changing computation order changes what a single model can do.

The demonstrations cover tree-constrained dependency parsing, convolutional image classification, and sequence completion with attention. By varying computation order, a single undirected network can serve as both a classifier and a prototype generator, and the framework can fill missing portions of a sequence. These examples show how flexible interactions among variables can support several uses of a learned model within one architectural framework.
icml-2022-modeling-structure-with-undire.tldr: Undirected neural networks combine factor-graph modularity with neural representations to support flexible computation orders and multiple model uses.

paragraphs: Useful uncertainty estimates should be accurate about uncertainty and precise enough to inform decisions. Recalibration uses held-out data to improve those estimates, but many methods require the starting model to already produce probabilities. Modular conformal calibration, or MCC, extends this approach to any regression model by turning it into a calibrated probabilistic predictor.

The framework is modular, allowing adjustments to existing algorithms that produce well-behaved predictive distributions. It also unifies isotonic recalibration, conformal calibration, and conformal interval prediction as instances of the same framework. This connection lets the authors apply their finite-sample calibration guarantees to those established methods as well as to newly designed MCC algorithms.

An empirical study on 17 regression datasets finds that the new algorithms achieve nearly perfect calibration and sharper predictions than existing methods. Sharpness matters because uncertainty predictions must remain informative as well as accurate. The paper therefore contributes both broader access to probabilistic prediction and a common theoretical structure for studying calibration methods, with empirical evidence that useful precision can improve.
icml-2022-modular-conformal-calibration-.tldr: Modular conformal calibration converts regression models into calibrated probabilistic predictors with finite-sample guarantees and improved empirical sharpness.

paragraphs: An online learner may face many alternatives that differ only slightly from one another. Those similarities can make their losses closely related. Standard bandit algorithms may then spend too much effort exploring numerous versions of a poor choice. The paper studies this issue when alternatives have a nested hierarchy of similarities.

The proposed nested exponential weights algorithm organizes exploration into layers. It selects alternatives through a sequence of nested decisions, using the hierarchy in the selection process. This adapts the exponential-weights approach to the structure of the alternatives instead of allowing many similar, suboptimal options to consume excessive exploration.

The authors establish a series of tight regret bounds for this adversarial bandit setting. The bounds show that a high degree of similarity can be used to resolve these learning problems efficiently. The result also addresses the red-bus/blue-bus issue: closely related alternatives should not distort decision-making merely through their multiplicity. The contribution makes the organization of the choice set an explicit part of the learning algorithm and its guarantees.
icml-2022-nested-bandits-697b129fd5.tldr: Nested exponential weights uses hierarchical similarities among alternatives to avoid redundant exploration and achieve tight regret bounds.

paragraphs: Learning with many interacting agents can require a number of samples that grows exponentially with the number of participants. This paper investigates sample-efficient, model-free reinforcement learning algorithms that work without centralized coordination. It considers different equilibrium objectives in different classes of Markov games rather than proposing one algorithm for every setting.

For general-sum Markov games, the authors develop stage-based V-learning methods for learning correlated or coarse correlated equilibria. These simplify earlier designs and analyses by avoiding a complicated weighted-regret bandit subroutine. For Markov potential games, they instead propose independent policy gradient with a decentralized, momentum-based technique for reducing variance, targeting Nash equilibria.

Each agent uses only local information to make decisions. Learning requires neither communication between agents nor a central coordinator, making the approach naturally applicable to larger groups. Numerical simulations corroborate the theoretical findings. The contribution combines simpler algorithms for one equilibrium-learning problem with a variance-reduced method for another, while maintaining the same decentralized information requirement across both.
icml-2022-on-improving-model-free-algori.tldr: The paper develops simpler and sample-efficient equilibrium-learning algorithms in which agents learn from local information without communication.

paragraphs: Vision models frequently encounter deliberately modified images during training and evaluation. These modifications can introduce artificial information alongside the changes they are intended to create. The paper examines two common assumptions: that such artifacts harm training, and that they are negligible when modified images are used to analyze a model.

The authors find that these assumptions fail in some cases and can lead to incorrect conclusions. They show bias in existing methods for identifying shape preference and in measures of robustness to occlusion. For occlusion robustness, they propose a fairer alternative. This matters because an evaluation intended to reveal model behavior can also reflect information introduced by the evaluation procedure.

Further experiments investigate how augmentation affects learning in vision models. Based on their empirical results, the authors argue for understanding and exploiting artifacts rather than automatically eliminating them. The claim is contextual: artificial information can affect both learning and measurement, and its role needs examination. The paper thus challenges assumptions about modification artifacts through evidence about training and evaluation.
icml-2022-on-the-effects-of-artificial-d.tldr: Artificial image modifications can bias evaluations and influence learning in useful ways, challenging common assumptions about their artifacts.

paragraphs: Classical simulation of a quantum circuit can require contracting a large network of tensors. The order in which those contractions are performed can dramatically change the computational cost. Finding a good order is difficult because there are many possible sequences, making this a challenging combinatorial optimization problem.

The paper proposes a reinforcement-learning agent whose policy is built around a graph neural network. This lets the decision-making model operate on the network structure involved in the contraction problem. The authors emphasize three obstacles: the enormous search space, a heavy-tailed reward distribution, and the difficulty of assigning credit to decisions within a contraction sequence.

A carefully implemented agent addresses these challenges and produces significant improvements over state-of-the-art techniques across three varieties of quantum circuits. The evaluation includes networks at the largest scales used in contemporary quantum computing. These findings support learning a graph-based contraction policy as a practical approach to reducing the computational burden of circuit simulation through better contraction ordering.
icml-2022-optimizing-tensor-network-cont.tldr: A reinforcement-learning agent with a graph neural network learns improved tensor contraction orders for classical quantum-circuit simulation.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows clients to train collaboratively while retaining their data locally. A single shared model may nevertheless fit clients poorly when their data distributions differ. This paper proposes personalization through local memorization, using the shared model's learned representations to connect collective learning with each client's own examples.

The method combines predictions from a collectively trained global model and a local k-nearest-neighbors model. The local model uses embeddings supplied by the global network, taking advantage of neural networks' ability to extract useful vector representations from images and text. Personalization comes from interpolating these two sources of predictions: shared knowledge and similarity to locally stored data.

The authors derive generalization bounds for binary classification. Across a suite of federated datasets, the method achieves significantly higher accuracy and fairness than the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. The theoretical result is specific to binary classification, while the empirical study evaluates the personalization mechanism on federated datasets. Together, they support local memorization as a way to make shared representations useful for heterogeneous clients.
icml-2022-personalized-federated-learnin.tldr: Combining a global federated model with local nearest-neighbor predictions improves reported personalization accuracy and fairness.

paragraphs: Finite mixture models represent a distribution through several components, whose parameters may be estimated at different speeds as data accumulates. Wasserstein distance is useful for analyzing these estimates because it accommodates interchangeable component labels and components whose weights vanish. However, it can hide differences between the remaining components by reflecting only their slowest convergence rate.

The authors penalize the log-likelihood to discourage mixing weights from vanishing. Under this setup, they derive stronger loss functions that distinguish how quickly different fitted components converge. These measures sharpen existing pointwise and uniform convergence results across several classes of mixture models, revealing behavior that a single worst-case rate obscures.

The results imply that a subset of components in the penalized maximum likelihood estimate typically converges substantially faster than earlier analyses suggested. Some conclusions also carry over to the ordinary, unpenalized estimator. A simulation study supports the theory. The main advance is a finer description of estimation error, allowing different components' statistical behavior to be visible within the same fitted model.
icml-2022-refined-convergence-rates-for-.tldr: New loss functions reveal that some estimated mixture components converge faster than Wasserstein-based analyses indicate.

paragraphs: The paper develops a point-cloud learning method built from neurons with spherical decision surfaces. These neurons arise through a conformal embedding of Euclidean space. Focusing on three-dimensional geometry, the authors investigate how their responses can be transformed predictably when the input rotates, providing a route to rotation-aware learning.

They derive a three-dimensional steerability constraint from the neurons' isometry property. After training the spherical neurons to classify point clouds in a canonical orientation, they use a tetrahedron basis to create four versions of each neuron. These form spherical filter banks whose outputs transform equivariantly with rotations.

The derived constraint then allows the filter-bank outputs to be interpolated into a rotation-invariant network. Equivariance provides predictable changes in intermediate responses, while invariance makes the final network insensitive to rotation. Tests on a synthetic point set and real-world three-dimensional skeleton data verify the theoretical findings. The contribution connects a specific neuron geometry to an explicit construction for handling rotated point clouds after training in a canonical orientation.
icml-2022-steerable-3d-spherical-neurons.tldr: Spherical neurons and a tetrahedral filter construction yield rotation-equivariant responses and a rotation-invariant point-cloud network.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly selects an option and receives feedback only for that choice. This paper studies a changing-reward setting in which each option's expected payoff never decreases. That monotonicity is useful structure: although rewards are non-stationary, their evolution is more constrained than arbitrary changes over time.

The authors design separate algorithms for rested and restless versions of this setting, called R-ed-UCB and R-less-UCB. Their regret guarantees depend on properties of the particular problem instance. Under certain circumstances, the regret grows on the order of the time horizon raised to two-thirds, up to logarithmic factors. The qualification matters because that rate is not stated for every instance.

Experiments compare the algorithms with state-of-the-art non-stationary bandit methods on synthetic tasks and an online model-selection problem using a real-world dataset. The results illustrate the effectiveness of exploiting rising expected payoffs. The contribution combines algorithms tailored to this reward structure with instance-sensitive guarantees and empirical evidence across both constructed tasks and a practical selection problem.
icml-2022-stochastic-rising-bandits-156a.tldr: Algorithms for rested and restless rising bandits exploit non-decreasing expected rewards to obtain instance-dependent regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning requires an agent to infer its current task from experience and adapt its behavior quickly. The paper argues that transformers are suited to this role because they process long sequences and use attention weights that depend on context. It introduces TrMRL, a transformer-based agent organized around a memory-reinstatement mechanism.

TrMRL associates recent working memories and recursively builds an episodic memory through transformer layers. The authors show that self-attention computes a consensus representation minimizing Bayes risk at each layer. This representation provides meaningful features for choosing actions, connecting the architecture's attention mechanism to a decision-theoretic account of how experience is combined.

Experiments evaluate the agent in high-dimensional continuous-control environments involving locomotion and dexterous manipulation. TrMRL achieves comparable or better eventual performance, sample efficiency, and generalization outside the training distribution than the tested baselines. These results support the architecture in those environments. The contribution combines a memory-based interpretation of transformer computation, a theoretical property of attention, and empirical evidence for adaptation in control tasks.
icml-2022-transformers-are-meta-reinforc.tldr: TrMRL uses transformer attention to build task-relevant memories and achieves competitive or better meta-reinforcement-learning results in continuous control.

paragraphs: Associative memory models retrieve stored information from a related query. Many such models exist, including classical Hopfield networks, sparse distributed memories, and modern continuous Hopfield networks. This paper organizes them through a shared sequence of three operations: measuring similarity, separating candidate matches, and projecting to a retrieved memory.

Different choices of similarity and separation functions recover the different model families. The authors also extend a mathematical framework that expresses associative memory through neural dynamics with local computation. They derive a general energy function that serves as a Lyapunov function for those dynamics, giving the unified formulation a dynamical foundation as well as an operational one.

The framework then enables an empirical comparison of similarity measures beyond the commonly used dot product. Across many tasks, Euclidean- or Manhattan-distance-based similarities substantially improve retrieval robustness and memory capacity relative to existing models. These findings indicate that the similarity operation can materially affect practical memory performance. The contribution therefore both connects established architectures and identifies useful alternatives within their shared design space.
icml-2022-universal-hopfield-networks-a-.tldr: A unified associative-memory framework connects Hopfield-style models and shows empirical benefits from Euclidean and Manhattan similarity measures.
